entities.name: Pelagius II
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Pelagius II, the bishop of Rome from 26 November 579 to his death on 7 February 590, played a pivotal role in shaping the course of medieval Christianity. 

 Born into a prominent family, Pelagius II ascended to the papacy amidst a period of significant ecclesiastical turmoil, including the rise of the Byzantine Empire and the ongoing debates about monasticism. 

 His papacy was marked by a series of diplomatic efforts to strengthen ties with the Eastern Roman Empire, including the negotiation of a treaty with the Byzantine Emperor Tiberius II Constantine. 

 Pelagius II also oversaw a significant rebuilding effort in Rome, investing in the restoration of damaged churches and the construction of new monuments. 

 Despite his efforts to maintain stability, Pelagius II's papacy was cut short by a devastating plague that ravaged Europe, killing an estimated 25% of the population. 

 The legacy of Pelagius II can be seen in the continued influence of the Roman Catholic Church on Western civilization, as well as the ongoing debates about the nature of sin and redemption that he helped to reignite. 

 As the last bishop of Rome to be elected before the First Council of Constantinople, Pelagius II's papacy represented a turning point in the development of the papacy as a central institution of Western Christianity. 

 His papacy also had a lasting impact on the development of the Roman calendar, with the introduction of the Julian calendar in 45 BCE being a direct result of his predecessor, Pope Gregory XIII. 

 The complex web of alliances and rivalries that defined Pelagius II's papacy, including his relationships with the Byzantine Empire, the Eastern Orthodox Church, and the Frankish kingdoms, continues to fascinate historians and scholars today.
